511.event_title: The Montreal Protocol on ozone-depleting substances is signed
511.event: Governments meeting in Montreal signed a protocol to cut and eventually phase out the production and use of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and other chemicals that deplete the stratospheric ozone layer, even though these chemicals were widely used in refrigeration, aerosols and industry. The treaty came into force in 1989, was strengthened several times, and became the first United Nations treaty to be ratified by every country. CFCs were phased out worldwide by 2010.
511.explanation: Faced with useful but harmful products, the world's governments weighed the benefit against the damage and chose the course that protected life.
511.tie_back: The kural praises the one who weighs both the good and the harm in a matter and is drawn to do the good, which is what the parties to the Montreal Protocol did.
511._accuracy_note: Shows careful weighing of benefit and harm resolved in favour of the good, but by governments collectively rather than by a single person chosen for a task.

512.event_title: Sergei Witte's term as Russia's finance minister
512.event: As Russian minister of finance from 1892 to 1903, Sergei Witte oversaw construction of the Trans-Siberian Railway, encouraged foreign investment and industrial growth, and in 1897 put the ruble on the gold standard. Under him the state monopoly on the sale of spirits became the largest single source of government revenue. He was dismissed in 1903 after palace intrigue.
512.explanation: Witte was judged by results: he widened the state's income, turned it into railways and industry, and stabilised the currency.
512.tie_back: The kural asks for someone who can widen the sources of income, turn them into lasting prosperity and deal with obstacles, which describes Witte's work as finance minister.
512._accuracy_note: A strong match for the kural's three tests of an economic administrator, though some of Witte's revenue methods, like the spirits monopoly, are open to criticism.

513.event_title: Garibaldi hands southern Italy to Victor Emmanuel and goes home to Caprera
513.place: Naples, Italy, and the island of Caprera, Sardinia
513.event: After conquering Sicily and Naples with his volunteers in 1860, Giuseppe Garibaldi held plebiscites and handed the whole of southern Italy to King Victor Emmanuel II, meeting him on 26 October 1860 and giving up his dictatorship of the South. He was the first to hail Victor Emmanuel as king of a united Italy. Immediately afterwards he returned to his farm on Caprera, refusing the rewards offered to him.
513.explanation: Garibaldi combined loyalty to the cause, military skill and decisive action with a striking lack of personal greed.
513.tie_back: The kural names loyalty, knowledge, decisiveness and freedom from greed as the marks of a trustworthy agent, and Garibaldi's handover and refusal of rewards display all four.
513._accuracy_note: A close fit to all four qualities, especially freedom from greed; Garibaldi was a volunteer commander rather than an appointed official.

514.event_title: Thomas Becket turns from royal chancellor to opponent of Henry II
514.event: Thomas Becket had served Henry II as chancellor and was the king's close friend, and in 1162 Henry had him made Archbishop of Canterbury. Soon afterwards Becket gave up the chancellorship against the king's wishes and began defending the rights of the Church against the crown. The dispute came to a head over the Constitutions of Clarendon of 1164, and Becket went into exile in France until 1170.
514.explanation: A man the king knew intimately and had tested for years became a very different person once he held the new office.
514.tie_back: The kural says that even people tested and approved in every way often turn out differently once they are actually doing the work, as Becket did after becoming archbishop.
514._accuracy_note: Very close to the kural's claim, though Becket's change is often seen as a turn toward principle rather than toward corruption.

515.event_title: Prussian reformers open the officer corps to merit
515.event: After Prussia's crushing defeat by Napoleon in 1806, a reform commission led by Gerhard von Scharnhorst, himself not of Prussian noble birth, reorganised the army. The reformers opened the officer corps, previously drawn almost entirely from the nobility, to middle-class candidates and made advancement depend on merit and education. They also founded military schools and developed the modern general staff.
515.explanation: A state that had lost a war with officers chosen by birth decided to choose them for knowledge and ability instead.
515.tie_back: The kural says a task should go to the one who knows how to do it and can see it through, not to someone favoured for other reasons, which is the principle the Prussian reformers adopted.
515._accuracy_note: Fits competence over favour well, though the reform concerned privilege of birth more than personal favouritism, and it was only partly carried through.

516.event_title: Ferdinand and Isabella back Columbus after the fall of Granada
516.event: Christopher Columbus sought support from Ferdinand and Isabella from 1486, and they had a commission examine his proposal while they were fighting the war against Granada. After at least two rejections, he obtained royal support in January 1492, soon after Granada surrendered on 2 January. In April 1492 he was granted the title Admiral of the Ocean Sea, and he sailed in August.
516.explanation: The monarchs examined both the man and the plan, and committed to it only when their war was over and resources were free.
516.tie_back: The kural says to size up the doer, then the deed, and then act when both fit the right time, and the monarchs' long-delayed decision followed that order.
516._accuracy_note: Shows examination of person, project and timing, but the sources do not record the monarchs' reasoning in detail, so the fit rests on the sequence of events.

517.event_title: Lincoln leaves the 1864 campaign plans to Grant
517.event: After appointing Ulysses S. Grant general-in-chief of the Union armies in March 1864, President Abraham Lincoln wrote to him on 30 April, the eve of Grant's spring campaign. In the letter Lincoln said he did not know and did not seek to know the details of Grant's plans, and that he was content to leave them to him. Grant crossed the Rapidan River with the Army of the Potomac days later, beginning the campaign that led to the end of the war.
517.explanation: After years of interfering with generals who failed him, Lincoln found one he trusted and left the work in his hands.
517.tie_back: The kural says that once you have decided this person will do this task by these means, you should hand the task to him and leave it with him, as Lincoln did with Grant.
517._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's call to delegate fully once the right person has been found.

518.event_title: Napoleon III makes Haussmann prefect of the Seine
518.event: Emperor Napoleon III appointed Georges-Eugene Haussmann prefect of the Seine in 1853, in effect the administrator of Paris, with the task of transforming the city. Over the next seventeen years Haussmann cut broad boulevards through old districts, greatly expanded the sewers and water supply, and created new parks. He raised large loans with little oversight and was dismissed in 1870 when a more liberal government came in.
518.explanation: Napoleon III gave one administrator both the task and the authority and money to carry it out, and Paris was remade as a result.
518.tie_back: The kural says that once a person's fitness for a task is established he should be made fully responsible for it with the authority that goes with it, which is how Haussmann was empowered.
518._accuracy_note: A clear case of conferring both task and authority, though the lack of checks on Haussmann's finances shows the risk of that approach.

519.event_title: Sultan Muhammad III has his minister Mahmud Gawan executed
519.event: Mahmud Gawan served the Bahmani sultans for many years as chief minister, and under him the sultanate reached its greatest size and degree of central control. Rival nobles falsified evidence, including a forged letter, to make him appear a traitor, and Sultan Muhammad III ordered his execution in 1481. Many nobles then withdrew from the court, and the effective power of the Bahmani state rapidly dissolved.
519.explanation: A ruler who let others turn him against his most devoted minister lost the support that held his kingdom together.
519.tie_back: The kural warns that fortune leaves the ruler who grows suspicious of a servant devoted to his work, and the Bahmani kingdom's collapse after Gawan's death shows it.
519._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation: slanderers poison the ruler's mind against a devoted minister, and the kingdom's prosperity departs.

520.event_title: The Yongzheng Emperor and the palace memorial system
520.event: The Yongzheng Emperor of the Qing dynasty expanded and regularised the palace memorial system, under which trusted officials across the empire sent confidential reports directly to him. He wrote his replies on them personally in vermilion ink before they were returned to the sender. Britannica describes him as an able ruler who checked corruption and personally scrutinised and directed all important matters of government.
520.explanation: Yongzheng kept a continual, personal watch on what his officials were doing, and his reign is known for its campaign against corruption.
520.tie_back: The kural tells the ruler to look into the conduct of those doing his work every day, because if they do not go crooked the world will not, and Yongzheng's memorial system was built for that daily scrutiny.
520._accuracy_note: A strong institutional parallel to daily supervision of officials, though the sources do not show that he read reports literally every day.
